pradeep|Physics|0|3|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Any object on a circular path needs a net inward force, and that force has a name.
**Step 1 — recall what circular motion requires.** Even at constant speed the velocity is
always turning, so there is an acceleration of magnitude v²/r directed **towards the
centre** ✓ By Newton's second law a force must produce it.
**Step 2 — name it.** The net inward force needed to keep a body on a circular path is
called the **centripetal force** ✓ It is defined by its **direction and role**, not by
its origin.
**Step 3 — see why the other three are only examples.** Centripetal force is a **job**
that some real force must do, and different situations hand the job to different forces:
**gravity** holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth
**friction** holds a car on an unbanked bend
**tension** holds a stone whirling on a string
**the electrostatic force** holds an electron near a nucleus
**the normal reaction** does it on a banked track or a wall of death
In each case the force **is** the centripetal force for that motion ✓
**Why "friction" cannot be the general answer.** It is right only for one special case -
a car turning on a flat road ✓ A satellite in vacuum feels no friction at all, yet moves
in a circle, so friction cannot be what is responsible in general.
**Why "gravitational force" cannot be either.** It accounts for orbits but not for a
stone on a string, where gravity acts **downward** while the circle is horizontal ✓
**What "mechanical force" would mean.** It is not a defined category in mechanics, so it
cannot be the answer to a question of naming ✗
**The one thing to be careful about.** Centripetal force is not an **extra** force added
to a free-body diagram. It is the **resultant** of the real forces, resolved along the
radius ✓ Drawing it alongside tension or gravity double-counts the same push.
∴ centripetal force.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, friction force. Friction supplies the
centripetal force only in the special case of a car on a flat bend; the Moon, a whirling
stone and an orbiting satellite all travel circles with no friction acting. The force
responsible in general is the centripetal force, so the key has been corrected to the
third option.

pradeep|Physics|0|4|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Angular acceleration and tangential acceleration are related exactly as ω and v are.
**Step 1 — recall the link.** Differentiating v = ωr with r constant:
a = αr
where a is the **tangential (linear) acceleration** and α the **angular acceleration**.
**Step 2 — rearrange and substitute.**
α = a/r
= 5/2
= **2·5 rad s⁻²** ✓
**Why the sign is positive.** The particle is said to be **accelerated**, so the speed is
increasing and α points along the direction of rotation ✓ There is nothing in the problem
to make it negative.
**Checking the units.** m s⁻² ÷ m = **s⁻²**, and since the radian is dimensionless that
is rad s⁻² ✓ a genuine angular acceleration.
**What this acceleration does.** The tangential part changes the **speed**; the separate
centripetal part, ω²r, changes the **direction** ✓ They are perpendicular, and the total
acceleration is their vector sum, √(a_t² + a_c²). The question asks only about the
tangential one.
**A worked instance.** Starting from rest with α = 2·5 rad s⁻²:
after 2 s, ω = αt = **5 rad s⁻¹** and v = ωr = **10 m s⁻¹**
and directly, v = at = 5 x 2 = **10 m s⁻¹** ✓ the two routes agree.
**Why the answer is not zero.** α = 0 would mean the speed never changes - that is
**uniform** circular motion, and the question explicitly gives a linear acceleration of
5 m s⁻² ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0** ✗ describes uniform circular motion. **−2·5 rad s⁻²**
✗ has the right size but describes a **slowing** particle. **None of these** ✗ would be
right only if 5/2 failed to appear among the options, and it does appear ✓
∴ 2·5 rad/s².

Note: the printed key gives the fourth option, "none of these". But α = a/r = 5/2 =
2·5 rad s⁻², which is exactly the second option, so the key has been corrected to it.

pradeep|Physics|0|5|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Linear velocity in rotation is the **cross product** v̄ = ω̄ x r̄, so this is a
determinant to evaluate.
**Step 1 — write the determinant.** With ω̄ = (2, −4, 1) and r̄ = (1, 1, 1):
v̄ = | î ĵ k̂ ; 2 −4 1 ; 1 1 1 |
**Step 2 — expand along the top row.**
î component: (−4)(1) − (1)(1) = −4 − 1 = **−5**
ĵ component: −[(2)(1) − (1)(1)] = −(2 − 1) = **−1**
k̂ component: (2)(1) − (−4)(1) = 2 + 4 = **+6**
**Step 3 — assemble.**
**v̄ = (−5î − ĵ + 6k̂) m s⁻¹** ✓
**Watch the middle sign.** The ĵ term carries a **minus** in the cofactor expansion ✓
Forgetting it turns −1 into +1 and is the single commonest error in a cross product.
**Check 1 — the result must be perpendicular to ω̄.**
v̄ · ω̄ = (−5)(2) + (−1)(−4) + (6)(1)
= −10 + 4 + 6
= **0** ✓
**Check 2 — it must also be perpendicular to r̄.**
v̄ · r̄ = −5 − 1 + 6 = **0** ✓
Both checks pass, which is strong confirmation: a cross product is perpendicular to each
of its factors, and only one option can satisfy both.
**Testing the distractors with the same check.**
(î + 3ĵ + 6k̂): dotted with r̄ = 1 + 3 + 6 = **10** ≠ 0 ✗
(3î − 3ĵ + 6k̂): dotted with r̄ = 3 − 3 + 6 = **6** ≠ 0 ✗
(î + ĵ + 6k̂): dotted with r̄ = 1 + 1 + 6 = **8** ≠ 0 ✗
Only (−5î − ĵ + 6k̂) is perpendicular to r̄ ✓ so the dot-product test alone settles the
question without redoing the determinant.
**Why the order matters.** It is ω̄ x r̄, not r̄ x ω̄ - reversing them flips every sign ✓
∴ (−5î − ĵ + 6k̂) m/s.

Note: the printed key gives the third option. Expanding the determinant gives
(−5, −1, 6), and the two perpendicularity checks confirm it while ruling the third option
out, so the key has been corrected to the second option.

pradeep|Physics|0|6|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Angular velocity is the time derivative of angular displacement.
**Step 1 — differentiate.** With θ(t) = 25t³ + 3t + 7:
ω = dθ/dt
= 75t² + 3
**Step 2 — substitute t = 2 s.**
ω = 75(2²) + 3
= 75(4) + 3
= 300 + 3
= **303 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Why the constant 7 disappears.** It is the angular position at t = 0 and does not
change with time, so it contributes nothing to the rate ✓ Only the **changing** part of
θ matters.
**Where each term comes from.**
d(25t³)/dt = **75t²** - the dominant term, growing with time
d(3t)/dt = **3** - a constant contribution
d(7)/dt = **0** ✓
**Checking numerically.** Over a short interval around t = 2:
θ(2) = 25(8) + 6 + 7 = **213 rad**
θ(2·01) = 25(8·1206) + 6·03 + 7 = **216·045 rad**
difference 3·045 rad in 0·01 s gives ω ≈ **304·5 rad s⁻¹** ✓ agreeing with 303 to the
accuracy of so crude a difference, and nowhere near 400 or 100.
**The angular acceleration, for completeness.**
α = dω/dt = 150t, which at t = 2 is **300 rad s⁻²** ✓ a rapidly accelerating rotation,
consistent with the large cubic term.
**Reading the distractors.** **400** ✗ and **100** ✗ match no step of the
differentiation. **Zero** ✗ would require θ to be constant, which it plainly is not ✓
**A quick order check.** At t = 2 the cubic term alone contributes 75(4) = 300, so the
answer must be a little **over** 300 - which immediately identifies 303 ✓
∴ 303 rad/sec.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, 400 rad/sec. Differentiating gives
ω = 75t² + 3, so ω(2) = 303, confirmed by the numerical difference above. The key has
been corrected to the first option.

pradeep|Physics|0|16|Pradeep Physics · C.s:
"Uniform" fixes the **speed**, not the velocity - and that distinction is the whole
question.
**Step 1 — look at the velocity.** The velocity is always **tangential**, and the tangent
turns continuously as the particle goes round ✓ Its **magnitude** is constant but its
**direction** changes at every instant, so the velocity **changes** ✓
**Step 2 — look at the acceleration.** The acceleration is centripetal, of magnitude
ω²r, directed **towards the centre**. Its magnitude too is constant, but it points at a
different direction at every point of the circle ✓ So the acceleration **changes** as
well.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Both velocity and acceleration change** ✓
**The point being tested.** Velocity and acceleration are **vectors**: a vector is
constant only if **both** its magnitude and its direction are fixed ✓ In uniform circular
motion neither vector qualifies, even though both **magnitudes** are constant.
**Seeing it in the algebra.** For r̄ = r(cos ωt, sin ωt):
v̄ = rω(−sin ωt, cos ωt) - magnitude rω, fixed; direction rotating ✓
ā = −rω²(cos ωt, sin ωt) - magnitude rω², fixed; direction rotating ✓
Each vector sweeps steadily round a circle of its own, never settling.
**A concrete check.** A particle going round a circle:
at the east point, the velocity points **north** and the acceleration **west**
a quarter turn later, at the north point, the velocity points **west** and the
acceleration **south** ✓
Both have turned through 90° - plainly not constant.
**What is constant in uniform circular motion.** The **speed**, the **magnitude** of the
acceleration, the **angular velocity** ω and the **kinetic energy** ✓ Those are the
scalars; the vectors all vary.
**Reading the distractors.** Every other option holds at least one of the two vectors
constant ✗ and each fails for the reason set out above ✓ In particular, "velocity is
constant and acceleration changes" confuses speed with velocity - the most common error
in this topic.
∴ both velocity and acceleration change.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, that both are constant. Velocity and
acceleration are vectors, and both rotate continuously as shown above, so neither is
constant. The key has been corrected to the fourth option.

pradeep|Physics|0|17|Pradeep Physics · C:
Angular velocity is 2π radians divided by the time for one complete turn.
**Step 1 — identify the period.** The Earth rotates once on its axis in **one day**:
T = 24 h
= 24 x 60 x 60
= **86400 s**
**Step 2 — apply ω = 2π/T.**
**ω = 2π/86400 rad s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate it.**
ω = 6·283/86400
= **7·27 x 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹**
an extremely small number, as it should be for something that takes a whole day to turn
once ✓
**Why the units must be seconds.** ω is asked for in **rad/s**, so T must be in seconds ✓
Leaving T as 24 gives 2π/24, which is in rad per **hour** - one of the distractors, and
about 3600 times too large.
**A check against the Earth's surface speed.** At the equator, r = 6400 km:
v = ωr = (7·27 x 10⁻⁵)(6·4 x 10⁶)
= **465 m s⁻¹**, about 1675 km/h ✓
which is the familiar figure for the speed of the equator - good confirmation.
**A note on the sidereal day.** Strictly the Earth turns once relative to the stars in
**86164 s**, four minutes short of the solar day, because it also moves along its orbit ✓
The difference is 0·3% and well below the resolution of these options, so 86400 s is the
intended answer.
**Reading the distractors.** **2π/3600** ✗ is the angular velocity of the **hour hand's**
scale of time - one turn per hour. **2π/24** ✗ leaves the period in hours. **2π/6400** ✗
uses the Earth's **radius in km** as if it were a time - a dimensional impossibility ✓
**The general formula.** ω = 2π/T = 2πf for any rotation, and recognising which period
belongs to the body in question is all this problem asks ✓
∴ 2π/86400 rad/s.

pradeep|Physics|0|21|Pradeep Physics · C.s:
Combine the vectors component by component, then take the magnitude.
**Step 1 — list the components.**
Ā = (1, 2, 1)
B̄ = (2, 0, 3)
C̄ = (−2, 0, 4)
**Step 2 — add Ā and B̄.**
Ā + B̄ = (1 + 2, 2 + 0, 1 + 3) = **(3, 2, 4)**
**Step 3 — subtract C̄.** Subtracting means changing the sign of every component of C̄:
Ā + B̄ − C̄ = (3 − (−2), 2 − 0, 4 − 4)
= **(5, 2, 0)**
**Step 4 — take the magnitude.**
|Ā + B̄ − C̄| = √(5² + 2² + 0²)
= √(25 + 4)
= **√29** ✓
**Watch the k̂ components.** Ā and B̄ contribute 1 + 3 = 4, and C̄ contributes 4, so they
**cancel exactly** and the resultant has no k̂ part ✓ Missing that cancellation is the
likeliest route to a wrong answer here.
**Watch the î component of C̄.** It is **−2**, so subtracting it **adds** 2: 3 + 2 = 5 ✓
Treating it as +2 would give 1, and a magnitude of √5.
**Checking the size.** √29 ≈ **5·39**, which must be at least as large as the biggest
single component, 5 ✓ and not much larger, since the other components are small. That
rough test already favours √29 over √20 ≈ 4·47, which is **smaller** than the î
component alone and so impossible.
**Reading the distractors.** **√20** ✗ is impossible by the test just made. **√65** ✗ is
|Ā + B̄ + C̄| territory - what you get by adding C̄ instead of subtracting it in the k̂
component (5² + 2² + 8²= 93, or similar mis-signings). **√69** ✗ matches no consistent
combination ✓
**The method in one line.** Resolve, add and subtract **component by component**, then
apply √(x² + y² + z²) ✓ No vector problem of this kind needs anything more.
∴ √29.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, √20. Component by component the resultant
is (5, 2, 0), whose magnitude is √29; and √20 ≈ 4·47 is smaller than the î component
alone, so it cannot be a magnitude of this vector. The key has been corrected to the
second option.
